title: Grid DFS/BFS on LeetCode: islands
overview: A module of LeetCode practice built on one template: loop over every cell and start a DFS (or BFS) from each unvisited land cell. Small changes to that template count islands, measure their area or perimeter, add up values, or check a condition on the whole island with a flag.

concepts.explain: Double loop over cells; each unvisited land cell starts a search that marks its whole island.
concepts.snippet:
for i, for j:
  if(!vis[i][j] && grid[i][j]==1){ dfs(i,j); cnt++; }

concepts.explain: Add 1 per cell for area, `grid` value for fish, or edges touching water for perimeter.
Set `flag = true` before a search; the search sets it false if any cell breaks the rule (touches the border, lies on water in grid1, ...). Count the island only if the flag survived.
Even after the flag turns false, finish the search so the entire island is marked visited and not counted again later.
Each land cell contributes one unit for every side that faces water or the outside of the grid.
LeetCode creates the `Solution` object for you; member arrays like `vis` work, but reset them inside the method.

files.title: LeetCode 200 - Number of Islands
files.what: Classic component count on a `char` grid: every DFS start is a new island.
steps: Store the size in `n`, `m` and clear `vis`.
For each unvisited `'1'` cell: `dfs` and `islands++`.
`dfs` spreads to valid, unvisited `'1'` neighbours.
files.input_note: Driver format: `n m`, then the grid row by row. Cells are the characters `0`/`1`. LeetCode example 2.
files.watch_out: The grid holds characters, so compare with `'1'`, not `1`. The `n==0` check comes after `grid[0]` is read, so it would be too late for an empty grid.

check.q: Why compare with `'1'` here but with `1` in Max Area of Island?
check.a: This problem gives a `vector<vector<char>>`; the other gives `int`s.

files.title: LeetCode 695 - Max Area of Island
files.what: Same template, with a counter `cnt` that grows by one per cell; the biggest counter wins.
steps: Set `cnt = 0` before each new DFS.
`dfs` does `cnt++` for each land cell it enters.
After the call, `mx = max(cnt, mx)`.
Return `mx` (0 if there is no land).
files.input_note: Driver format: `n m`, then the grid row by row. LeetCode example 1.
files.output_note: `maxAreaOfIsland = 6`, the expected answer (diagonal cells do not join islands).

check.q: What does the function return for a grid of all zeros?
check.a: 0, because `mx` starts at 0 and no DFS runs.

files.title: LeetCode 2658 - Maximum Fish in a Grid

problem.name: LeetCode 2658 - Maximum Number of Fish in a Grid

files.what: Water cells (value > 0) form ponds; DFS adds up the fish in each pond and keeps the best total.
steps: Land is `0`, water is any value > 0.
Before each DFS: `total = 0`.
`dfs` adds `grid[si][sj]` and spreads to water neighbours.
Keep `mx = max(total, mx)`.
files.input_note: Driver format: `n m`, then the grid row by row. LeetCode example 1.
files.output_note: `findMaxFish = 7` (3 + 4 in the right-side pond), as expected.

check.q: How is this different from Max Area of Island?
check.a: It adds the cell values instead of adding 1 per cell.

files.title: LeetCode 463 - Island Perimeter (BFS)
files.what: BFS over the whole grid from (0,0); for every land cell it counts sides that face water or the border.
steps: Start BFS at (0,0) and move to any valid unvisited cell (land or water), so the whole grid is covered.
When the popped cell is land, check its 4 sides.
A side adds 1 to `perimeter` if it is outside the grid or water.
Return `perimeter`.
files.input_note: Driver format: `n m`, then the grid row by row. LeetCode example 1.
files.watch_out: It visits water cells too, which works but is extra work; the DFS versions only walk land.

check.q: Why must `!valid(ci, cj)` be checked before `grid[ci][cj] == 0`?
check.a: Short-circuit `||` stops before reading outside the grid.

files.title: Island Perimeter (DFS over all cells)
files.what: Same counting rule, but a DFS started from the first land cell; the DFS still steps into water cells.
steps: Find a land cell with the double loop and start `dfs` there.
Inside `dfs`, if the cell is land, count its water/border sides.
Recurse into any valid unvisited neighbour (land or water).
files.input_note: Driver format: `n m`, then the grid row by row. LeetCode example 1.
files.watch_out: Because it recurses into water too, recursion depth can reach n·m; V2 fixes that by walking only land.

check.q: What does the `grid[Ai][Aj] == 1` check inside `dfs` protect against?
check.a: Counting sides of water cells, which the DFS also visits.

files.title: Island Perimeter (DFS, land only)
files.what: Cleaner DFS: it only enters land cells, so every visited cell contributes its water/border sides.
steps: Start from a land cell.
Count each side that is outside the grid or water.
Recurse only into valid, unvisited land neighbours.
files.complexity: Time O(cells of the island) · Space O(same)
files.input_note: Driver format: `n m`, then the grid row by row. LeetCode example 1.
files.output_note: `islandPerimeter = 16`, same as the other two versions.

check.q: Another way to get the perimeter without any search?

files.title: LeetCode 1971 - Find if Path Exists

problem.name: LeetCode 1971 - Find if Path Exists in Graph

files.what: Builds an adjacency list from the edge array and DFS from `source`; `found` becomes true on reaching `destination`.
steps: Push every edge both ways into `adj`.
`dfs(node, destination, found)` marks `node`; if it is the destination, set `found = true` and return.
Otherwise recurse into unvisited children.
Return `found`.
files.complexity: Time O(n + e) · Space O(n + e)
files.input_note: Driver format: number of cases; each is `n e`, e edges, then `source destination`. LeetCode's two examples.
files.output_note: `true` then `false`, matching the examples (0 and 5 are in different pieces in example 2).
files.watch_out: The member arrays are big (200005 vectors), so the driver creates the object with `new`. Recursion depth can reach 2·10^5 on a long chain; BFS or DSU avoids deep recursion.

check.a: So every recursive call updates the same variable seen by `validPath`.

files.title: LeetCode 1905 - Count Sub Islands
files.what: Walks each island of `grid2`; if any of its cells is water in `grid1`, the flag turns false and it is not counted.
steps: For each unvisited land cell of `grid2`, set `flag = true` and DFS.
Inside DFS, if `grid1[si][sj] == 0`, set `flag = false` but keep going.
Spread only over land of `grid2`.
After the DFS, `cnt++` if `flag` is still true.
files.input_note: Driver format: `n m`, then grid1 rows, then grid2 rows. LeetCode example 1.
files.watch_out: Do not `return` as soon as the flag becomes false: the rest of the island would stay unvisited and be counted later as a separate island.

check.q: What makes an island of grid2 a sub-island?
check.a: Every one of its cells is also land in grid1.

files.title: LeetCode 1254 - Closed Islands (DFS)
files.what: Land is `0` here. An island is closed unless some cell of it has a neighbour outside the grid.
steps: For each unvisited `0` cell: `flag = true`, then DFS.
For each direction, if the neighbour is outside the grid, set `flag = false`.
Recurse into valid unvisited `0` neighbours.
Count the island if `flag` stayed true.
files.input_note: Driver format: number of cases, then `n m` and the grid for each. LeetCode examples 1 and 3.
files.watch_out: Values are flipped compared with other island problems: `0` is land, `1` is water.

check.q: How does the code know an island touches the edge?
check.a: One of its cells has a neighbour for which `valid` is false.

files.title: Closed Islands (BFS version)
files.what: The same flag idea written with a queue instead of recursion.
steps: Identical outer loop and flag.
`bfs` pops a cell and checks the 4 neighbours; an out-of-grid neighbour clears the flag.
Valid unvisited `0` neighbours are pushed and marked.
files.input_note: Same driver and input as the DFS version.
files.output_note: `2` and `2`, the same as the DFS version.

check.q: When is the BFS version safer than the DFS one?
check.a: On very large islands, where deep recursion could overflow the stack.

recap: One template solves most island problems: loop cells, search from unvisited land.
Change what you add inside the search: 1, the cell value, or water sides.
Use a flag for yes/no rules about a whole island, and finish the search anyway.
Check which value means land before you code.
BFS and DFS give the same answers here; BFS avoids deep recursion.

check_yourself.q: How would you count islands that touch the border?
check_yourself.a: Count islands where the flag became false (or count all minus closed ones).

check_yourself.q: Why reset `vis` inside the LeetCode method?
check_yourself.a: The judge may reuse the object for several tests; stale marks would give wrong answers.

check_yourself.q: What is the time complexity of any of these grid searches?
check_yourself.a: O(n·m): each cell is visited once and has 4 neighbours.
